newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico police find guerrilla safe house in Acapulco.
newsitem.headline: Mexico police find guerrilla safe house in Acapulco.

text.p: Police acting on an anonymous tip raided a house in the tourist resort of Acapulco on Tuesday and found weapons, propaganda and uniforms belonging to a Marxist guerrilla group, authorities said.
State police said the white-painted house was empty when they burst in and no members of the banned Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR) were arrested.

"At 1:30 in the afternoon we received an anonmyous call which told us (that in the house) there were explosive devices and arms and so immediately the regional commander ordered the area to be inspected," Francisco Vargas Najera, director of the state detective police, told reporters.

Gun-toting officials immediately sealed off the area around the house, located on an estate built for teachers. Police said the building, which had its windows darkened to prevent anyone seeing in, appeared to have been used as a safe house for rebels operating in the area.

Inside, police found bullet-proof jackets, computers used to write propaganda, videos and home-made grenades. The house belonged to a woman who had not been seen in the area for some time and was apparently renting it out, police sources said.
The EPR has been particularly active in Guerrero, a southwestern state which is home to the glitzy Pacific Coast beaches of Acapulco as well as to some of Mexico's poorest and most backward villages.

Since it made a first appearance at the end of June in Guerrero, the group has attacked in at least four states and claims to have killed more than 90 police and soldiers, though it has concentrated more on propaganda activities than military operations in recent weeks.
Authorities put the total of dead at less than 30 and claim to have dealt the group a heavy blow by arresting around 100 suspected members.
The guerrillas, however, say they retain strength in several states in central Mexico and may carry out a major attack in coming months.
EPR activity was also seen on Tuesday at the other end of Mexico in the northeast. Witnesses said a huge EPR banner was draped over a footbridge in the city of Ciudad Victoria.
It was the first time the guerrilla group had shown any signs of activity in the northeastern state of Tamaulipas, which borders Texas.
The banner, hoisted only a block away from the state headquarters of the Prosecutor-General's office, was quickly removed by police. No one was arrested.
